          <p>Direction B applied to the two highest-traffic surfaces.</p>
          <ul>
            <li>Rebuild the hero: install box with OS toggle, version in the button, DOM-rendered prompt.</li>
            <li>Promote Themes and Segments into primary nav; move Sponsor, Swag and Blog into Community.</li>
            <li>Retire the non-closeable announcement bar in favour of a footer sponsor block.</li>
            <li>Token pass: neutral ramp, type scale, chevron geometry, zoned dark sections.</li>
          </ul>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="phase">
        <span class="no">Phase 2</span>
        <div>
          <h4>The renderer</h4>
          <p>The load-bearing investment. One function: config + mock context → DOM.</p>
          <ul>
            <li>Reuse <code>segment_data.json</code> as the fixture context; it already covers every segment.</li>
            <li>Verify fidelity against the Go engine in CI — render every bundled theme both ways and diff the ANSI.</li>
            <li>Ship it first as a build-time renderer, so there is no client-side cost yet.</li>
          </ul>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="phase">
        <span class="no">Phase 3</span>
        <div>
          <h4>Catalogs</h4>
          <p>Point the renderer at the two large surfaces.</p>
          <ul>
            <li><code>/themes</code>: faceted gallery, per-theme URLs, live renders, one-click apply command. Deletes 8 MB of PNGs.</li>
            <li><code>/segments</code>: faceted catalog with badge column, each card previewing its own output.</li>
            <li>Embed the same preview at the top of every segment reference page.</li>
          </ul>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="phase">
        <span class="no">Phase 4</span>
        <div>
          <h4>Docs restructure</h4>
          <p>IA-2 in full, once the two catalogs have left <code>/docs</code>.</p>
          <ul>
            <li>Split the FAQ into Troubleshooting by shell, terminal and editor.</li>
            <li>Separate hand-written Configure prose from a generated Reference tier — the Bun split.</li>
            <li>Drop emoji from sidebar labels; order segments by usage, not alphabet.</li>
          </ul>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="phase">
        <span class="no">Phase 5</span>
        <div>
          <h4>Studio, if the renderer holds up</h4>
          <p>Only worth starting once phases 2–3 have proven fidelity in production.</p>
          <ul>
            <li>Editor around the existing renderer; config encoded in the URL.</li>
            <li>“Open in Studio” from every theme and every segment page.</li>
            <li>Short-link service so <code>--config</code> can point at a shared prompt.</li>
          </ul>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ══════════════════════════════ OPEN ══════════════════════════════ -->
<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap stack gap-6">
    <div class="stack gap-3">
      <p class="eyebrow">07 — Open questions</p>
      <h2 style="font-size:1.65rem;">Decisions that change the plan</h2>
    </div>
    <div class="findings">
      <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Q1</span><p><b>Stay on Docusaurus?</b> Astro + Starlight is what Biome and Tauri run, and it makes custom app-like pages far cheaper than Docusaurus swizzling. Migrating 153 docs is real work but mostly mechanical. Direction B is doable either way; direction C is materially easier on Astro.</p></div>
      <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Q2</span><p><b>Second renderer, or compile the real one?</b> A JS renderer risks drifting from the Go engine. The alternative is compiling the engine to WASM and rendering the truth — heavier, but there is then only one implementation to trust.</p></div>
      <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Q3</span><p><b>Nerd Font glyphs on the web.</b> Live previews need a subset Nerd Font served from the site, or the powerline separators will render as tofu for most visitors. Licensing and weight both need a look.</p></div>
      <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Q4</span><p><b>Does the blog stay?</b> Six posts since 2022. Either fold it into a Community section alongside release notes, or retire it and let the changelog carry that job.</p></div>
      <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Q5</span><p><b>Where does sponsorship live?</b> The permanent announcement bar and the two primary-nav slots are the most valuable real estate on the site and currently earn less than a well-placed footer block would.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<footer class="end">
  <div class="wrap">Analysis phase only — no code changed. Mockups are DOM, not images; view source to lift the chevron geometry.</div>
</footer>

</div>

<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap stack gap-8">
    <div class="stack gap-3">
      <p class="eyebrow">01 — Where we are</p>
      <h2 style="font-size:1.65rem;">The homepage is still the 2020 Docusaurus scaffold</h2>
      <p class="lede">
        Two buttons, three emoji paragraphs, one static PNG — about 130 lines total. Everything that would
        make a visitor install has to be found somewhere else.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="stat-grid">
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">130</span><span class="l">lines in the entire homepage</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">11</span><span class="l">top-level sidebar entries, all emoji-prefixed</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">28,093<span style="font-size:0.6em">px</span></span><span class="l">height of the themes page — 124 PNGs, 8 MB, no filter</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">0</span><span class="l">segment reference pages showing what the segment looks like</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n">117</span><span class="l">segments, reachable only by guessing a category</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="n warn">3</span><span class="l">clicks minimum from homepage to an install command</span></div>
    </div>

    <div class="stack gap-4">
      <h3 style="font-size:1.05rem;">Concrete defects found in the codebase</h3>
      <div class="findings">
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>“Get Started →” lands on a theory page.</b> <code>configuration/introduction.mdx</code> carries <code>slug: /</code>, so the primary homepage CTA opens an essay about blocks and segments — not an install command. The sidebar’s actual first item is Getting Started › Installation › Windows, which the CTA never reaches.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>No index pages exist.</b> Getting Started, Segments, and all eight segment sub-groups are bare categories — clicking them only expands a tree. <code>static/llms.txt</code> already links <code>/docs/segments/overview</code> and <code>/docs/configuration/overview</code>; neither page exists, and <code>onBrokenLinks: 'ignore'</code> hides it.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev block">Blocking</span>
          <p><b>Segment discovery depends on guessing a bucket.</b> <code>kubectl</code>, <code>helm</code> and <code>argocd</code> live under CLI, not Cloud. <code>docker</code> is CLI. <code>winget</code> is System. Every group is <code>collapsed: true</code> by default, so the default view of 117 segments shows nothing.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>The theme gallery is one 124-image scroll.</b> No search, no tags, no filter, no per-theme URL, no way to apply one. The Nerd-Font requirement is a sentence of prose, not a facet. It is also one of only two homepage CTAs.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>The FAQ absorbs everything with no home.</b> 24 headings covering PowerShell, fonts, Windows Terminal, JetBrains, Conda, venv, Zsh, Fish, Xonsh, Vim and posh-git. There is no troubleshooting section, no per-shell page and no per-terminal page.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>Orphan and near-orphan docs.</b> <code>docs/auth.mdx</code> is in no sidebar — only reachable via an OAuth redirect. <code>Advanced</code> is a category with exactly one child. <code>dsc</code>, <code>themes</code>, <code>share</code>, <code>faq</code>, <code>migrating</code> and <code>contributors</code> float loose at root.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev friction">Friction</span>
          <p><b>Navbar priorities are inverted.</b> Sponsor and Swag sit in primary left nav beside Docs and Blog, above a non-closeable sponsor bar. The blog has averaged under one post a year since 2022. Themes and Segments — the two things people actually come for — are not in the nav at all.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="finding">
          <span class="sev polish">Polish</span>
          <p><b>The CSS has hash-coupled selectors.</b> <code>a.getStarted_Sjon</code> and <code>.themedImage_ToTc</code> target generated CSS-module hashes and break silently on upgrade. <code>--ifm-color-primary-lightest</code> is <code>rgb(8,9,10)</code> — near-black. <code>--ifm-font-family-monospace</code> is set to <code>"Inter"</code>. Fira Code is fetched from Google Fonts and never referenced.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

    <div class="stack gap-4">
      <h3 style="font-size:1.05rem;">The four idioms</h3>
      <div class="findings">
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 1</span><p><b>The hero is the install command.</b> Bun, Atuin, Astro and Tauri all put a copyable command above the fold, with an OS or package-manager toggle and the current version in the button. Nobody makes you click through.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 2</span><p><b>Product surfaces are rendered in the DOM, never screenshotted.</b> Crisp at any DPI, selectable, theme-reactive, diffable in git, indexable. PNG galleries now read as dated — which is exactly what our themes page is.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 3</span><p><b>Dark-first, but zoned.</b> One flat black is out. Warp tints section washes purple/blue/green/amber over a near-black ground; Atuin runs <code>#0f1722</code> with a green and warm-cream pair. Calibrated neutral ramps plus one saturated accent — no gradient mesh, no glass, no grain.</p></div>
        <div class="finding"><span class="sev polish">Idiom 4</span><p><b>Typography carries the brand.</b> Zed self-hosts four families; Ghostty picked Pretendard; Atuin pairs DM Sans with Space Mono. The sites that read as templates are the ones on stock Inter over a stock generator theme — Starship and Oh My Posh, both.</p></div>
      </div>
      <div class="callout">
        <b>Free win, one line:</b> Starship prepends <code>"Nerd Font"</code> to its monospace stack, so Nerd Font glyphs render correctly in code blocks for anyone who has the font installed. Every powerline character in our docs currently falls back to tofu for visitors without it.
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

Proposal live: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7e76d82e-c9b9-4c14-888b-d0e1f540d320**

Mockups are DOM — powerline chevrons cut with `clip-path`, no images. That itself is the argument.

## Core finding

Site sells a thing whose whole value is pixels on screen. Shows almost none of them. Starship has same disease (logo-only hero). Atuin, Zed, Bun all render product surfaces in DOM now — screenshots read as dated.

**Hard defects, not opinions:**
- `configuration/introduction.mdx` has `slug: /` — "Get Started →" lands on block/segment theory, not an install command. 3 clicks to a command.
- Zero index pages. `static/llms.txt` already links `/docs/segments/overview` + `/docs/configuration/overview`; neither exists. `onBrokenLinks: 'ignore'` hides it.
- Themes page: 28,093px, 124 PNGs, 8MB, no filter/tags/per-theme URL/apply.
- 117 segments, all groups `collapsed: true`, discovery = guess the bucket (`kubectl`/`helm`/`argocd` are CLI, not Cloud).
- `custom.css` targets generated hashes (`a.getStarted_Sjon`, `.themedImage_ToTc`). `--ifm-font-family-monospace: "Inter"`. `--ifm-color-primary-lightest: rgb(8,9,10)`. Fira Code fetched, never used.
- `auth.mdx` orphaned — no sidebar entry, reachable only via OAuth redirect.

## Three directions

| | A · Calibrated | B · Terminal Native | C · Studio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Effort | days | weeks | a quarter |
| IA | IA-1 Tidy | IA-2 Four doors | IA-3 Studio-first |
| Kills PNG gallery | no | yes | yes, editable |

**Recommend B + IA-2, built so C stays reachable.** Load-bearing piece in both is one prompt renderer: `config + mock context → DOM`. `segment_data.json` is already a complete fixture. `export_themes.mjs` already knows author + bg per theme. Build renderer once behind a stable interface; B uses it at build time, C later drives it from an editor.

IA-2 moves Themes and Segments *out* of `/docs` into faceted first-class sections, splits Configure prose from a generated Reference tier (Bun's move), and gives Sponsor/Swag/Blog an honest home in Community instead of primary nav.

## Open decisions that change the plan

1. Stay on Docusaurus, or move to Astro + Starlight (Biome, Tauri)? C is materially cheaper on Astro.
2. JS renderer (drift risk vs Go engine) or compile engine to WASM (one truth, heavier)?
3. Nerd Font subset served from site — otherwise live previews are tofu. Licensing + weight.
4. Blog: 6 posts since 2022. Fold into Community with release notes, or retire.

Phase 0 in the artifact is all bug fixes, no design calls — shippable immediately, independent of which direction you pick. Say the word and I'll plan it.

Now I'm structuring the answer: starting with where the pipeline logic currently lives, explaining why the web can't reuse it since it's all Go, pointing out that `--data` already makes the engine hermetic, laying out three options with a recommendation, and identifying what's missing—a structured export format instead of ANSI output.

content.text:
Today it comes from the Go binary. Nothing on the web renders anything.

## Current pipeline

[export_themes.mjs](website/export_themes.mjs) is a shell-out loop:

```
themes/*.omp.json
  → oh-my-posh config export image --config X --data segment_data.json
      --background-color Y --author Z
  → prompt.Engine.Primary()          ANSI string
  → cli/image/image.go               rasterize (fork of homeport/termshot,
                                      fogleman/gg + opentype)
  → website/static/img/themes/X.png
  → append markdown into docs/themes.md
```

Everything that decides what a prompt looks like is Go: [prompt/engine.go](src/prompt/engine.go) (864 lines), [config/segment.go](src/config/segment.go), `segments/*`, `template/`, `color/`, `terminal/writer.go`. `image.go` is 920 lines of rasterizer that exists only because there was no other way to get pixels into markdown.

No WASM build, no JS renderer, no render endpoint. Website has zero of it.

## The wedge already exists

[cli/data.go](src/cli/data.go) — `applyDataFile` sets `flags.SegmentData` + `flags.EnvData`, and segments replay from that instead of shelling out to `git`, `kubectl`, `az`. `segment_data.json` covers every segment.

That makes the engine **hermetic**: no exec, no filesystem walk, no HTTP. That's precisely the property a browser build needs. `--data` was built for screenshots, but it's the studio's foundation.

## Three ways to get it on the web

**1. WASM — single source of truth.** `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` build of the engine. With `SegmentData` populated the hot path already avoids exec/fs; cache and HTTP need stubs. Ship the config from the editor, get output back. No drift, ever.

**2. Render endpoint — cheapest.** `website/api` is already Azure Functions ([api/mcp](website/api/mcp), [api/auth](website/api/auth)). Add `/api/render`: POST config + data, shell the real binary, return output. Zero drift, zero WASM work, one round-trip per edit (debounce ~120ms). Also replaces the PNG build step for the gallery.

**3. TypeScript reimplementation — don't.** Template engine, 117 segments, color resolution, palettes, gradients, powerline joining. Guaranteed drift, and the drift is invisible until a user reports a wrong prompt.

## Missing piece either way

Both 1 and 2 return **ANSI**, so the browser needs an ANSI parser — same problem `image.go` already solved badly once.

Better: add a structured emitter alongside the image one. `terminal/writer.go` already tracks foreground, background, and style per run — it just flattens them to escape codes. Emit them instead:

```
config export render --format json --data segment_data.json
→ [{ "text": "alice", "fg": "#191724", "bg": "#eb6f92", "bold": true }, …]
```

Then JS maps runs to spans. No parser, no fidelity guesswork, and it's testable in Go against the same golden files the ANSI writer uses.

**Recommendation:** endpoint + structured export first (small, no drift, unblocks Phase 2–3 of the artifact). WASM later only if the studio needs sub-100ms interactive feedback. That ordering also lets you delete `cli/image/image.go` — 920 lines of rasterizer whose only consumer is the gallery you're replacing.

content.thinking:
The user is proposing moving the image generation entirely to a web service, which would let the CLI just POST the config and receive an image back—eliminating the need to ship image rendering dependencies in the binary. Now I'm thinking through whether the backend should use a TypeScript reimplementation or WebAssembly, and I'm realizing there are actually two distinct layers to consider: the evaluation layer that processes the config, and then the rendering layer that generates the image.

The evaluation layer—where the config and environment get transformed into styled runs with segments, templates, colors, and all the styling logic—is the complex semantic engine with 117 segments and a template language. Reimplementing that in TypeScript would risk drift from the Go original, so it needs to stay in Go, probably compiled to WebAssembly for the endpoint. The rendering layer, though—converting those styled runs into a PNG—is just font metrics and canvas drawing, which is genuinely portable and has no semantic risk. TypeScript with something like Satori or node-canvas would work fine here, and could even output SVG directly, which is cleaner and more themeable than rasterizing to PNG.

So the split should happen at the ANSI/structured-runs boundary: the endpoint runs the Go evaluation logic as WebAssembly to produce the styled runs, then uses TypeScript to render those runs into SVG or PNG.

Now for the question of whether to include image rendering in the shipped binary at all. There are a few approaches: a build tag to strip out the image dependencies, which creates two variants and the question of which one to ship; or making `config export image` always hit a remote endpoint, which removes the dependencies but breaks offline use and creates a privacy concern since configs and environment data could contain usernames, hostnames, paths, or cloud account identifiers that would be sent to the server.

A third option is a separate binary or plugin, keeping the main binary lean while preserving the offline story. Or I could emit SVG from Go instead of PNG — that drops all the heavy dependencies and works because terminal output is fundamentally a character grid. You only need one advance width constant per font size, not full font metrics, so an SVG emitter becomes a small, dependency-free implementation.

Let me check what image.go actually imports and measure the binary cost impact.

content.text:
Two different renderers hiding under one word. They have opposite answers.

| Layer | What it does | Reimplement in TS? |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaluation** | config + context → styled runs. 117 segments, template language, palettes, gradients, powerline joins | **No.** Drift is silent and user-visible |
| **Rasterization** | styled runs → pixels. [image.go](src/cli/image/image.go), 920 lines, forked termshot | **Yes, safely.** Worst case is a pixel diff, not a wrong prompt |

So: TS for the raster, Go for the evaluation. Which means WASM — but read the next part first, because it may make the raster question disappear.

## The imager is already less local than you think

[image.go:236-246](src/cli/image/image.go:236) downloads `Hack.zip` from the nerd-fonts GitHub release at runtime and caches it. `config export image` already requires network on first use. The offline argument against a thin client is weaker than it looks.

And [image.go:462](src/cli/image/image.go:462) shows the layout is a **character grid** — one `spaceAdvance` constant drives measurement, wrapping, and width. Not real typesetting.

## So don't move the imager to the web. Move the rasterizer out of the imager.

Emit **SVG from Go** instead of PNG:

- Grid geometry, one advance constant. ~150 lines.
- Drops `fogleman/gg`, `esimov/stackblur-go`, `golang.org/x/image/font/opentype`, `golang/freetype`, and the Hack.zip download.
- `config export image` stays fully local and gets *faster and more offline* than today.
- SVG is the interchange format for everything else: gallery assets (~2-5KB each vs 8MB of PNG), studio preview, endpoint output.
- PNG becomes a conversion step, done wherever convenient — `resvg-wasm` in the Function, or `--format png` shelling to nothing at all if you decide PNG is a web-only concern.

That reframes your question: you don't need TS-vs-WASM for the imager. You need it for the **studio**, where it's WASM, because the studio needs evaluation.

## Excluding it from the shipped binary

Ranked:

1. **SVG emitter, no exclusion needed.** The deps leave, the feature stays. No build tags, no second artifact, no infra dependency. Do this first.
2. **Build tag** (`//go:build !noimage`) — only worth it if the SVG emitter still costs more than you want. Two artifacts confuses users; you'd have to pick which one is "the" release.
3. **Thin client that POSTs to the endpoint** — last resort. Creates a hard runtime dependency on your infra for a CLI command, and see below.

## Before you build a public render endpoint

**The `http` segment takes an arbitrary URL from config properties** ([segments/http.go:27](src/segments/http.go:27)). So do `owm`, `nba`, `ipify`, `todoist`, `wakatime`. An endpoint that evaluates segments live is an open SSRF proxy — anyone can POST a config that makes your Azure Function fetch internal addresses and return the result.

Non-negotiable if you ship this:

1. **Data-replay only.** Force `flags.SegmentData` populated; hard-disable live segment resolution server-side. Not a config option — a compile-time or entrypoint guard.
2. **Cap and timeout.** Config size limit, template depth limit, render deadline. Gradients and templates are user-supplied compute.
3. **Rate limit per IP.** Unauthenticated image generation is a cheap amplification target.
4. **State the data flow.** Configs and `--data` files carry usernames, hostnames, paths, cloud subscription names. If `config export image` ever POSTs by default, that's a silent behavior change users can't see. Opt-in, or documented loudly.

## Suggested order

1. SVG emitter in Go, behind `config export image --format svg`. Local, no deps, no endpoint.
2. Switch the gallery to SVG. 8MB → ~300KB, crisp, theme-reactive. Delete the PNG pipeline.
3. Drop the rasterizer and its four deps once nothing consumes PNG locally.
4. `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` build of the engine — same SVG emitter, now in the browser. This is the studio.
5. Endpoint only if you still want `oh-my-posh-generate-image` as a service — and by then it's the wasm blob in a Function, with the guards above, not a shelled binary.

Steps 1–3 are pure wins with no new infrastructure. Step 4 is where the studio actually starts.

content.text:
Your second idea is the right one, and it's stronger than you framed it. Today's flow throws away information and then tries to recover it:

```
engine → terminal writer → ANSI string → image.go re-parses ANSI → pixels
```

`image.go` re-derives what the writer already computed. [image.go:498](src/cli/image/image.go:498) — *"Add additional width for Nerd Font glyphs"* — is a symptom: [terminal/writer.go:894](src/terminal/writer.go:894) already ran `countVisibleCells` through `go-runewidth`, and the imager redoes it worse. Every fidelity bug in the imager lives in that round-trip.

## But it isn't "add a writer" — there's no writer abstraction to add to

`terminal` is a 1243-line package with **global mutable state**: `builder`, `length`, `cellIndex`, `foregroundColor`, `currentColor`, `bgGradientCells`. `Write(bg, fg, txt)` appends into a package-level `strings.Builder`. Escape emission is interleaved with the logic that decides what to draw — `writeColorise`, `writeTransparentStart`, `writeEscapedAnsiParts` all bake `\x1b[` into the same pass as anchor scanning and gradient stamping.

So the actual move is one step earlier: **separate what to draw from how to encode it.**

```
engine
  → resolver   anchors, gradients, transparency, hyperlinks, cell widths
  → Run stream []Run{Text, FG, BG, Style, Link}
  → encoder    ansi | svg | json | plain
```

The resolver already exists inside the writer — `activeBackground()`, `activeForeground()`, `gradientCell()`, `countVisibleCells()`, `writeAnchorOverride()`. It just never surfaces its answers.

Extract the run stream and you get four encoders for the price of one:

- **ansi** — current behavior, must stay byte-identical
- **svg** — replaces all 920 lines of `image.go`, drops `gg`, `stackblur`, `opentype`, `freetype`, and the runtime Hack.zip download
- **json** — free, and it's exactly what the studio and any render endpoint want
- **plain** — currently a `Plain bool` threaded through the same pass; becomes an encoder

Window chrome isn't a reason to keep `image.go`: title bar, dots and author line are SVG decoration, and `stackblur` existed only for the drop shadow, which is `feDropShadow`.

## What stays worth having in the binary

One thing, and it's real: `config export image` **without** `--data` renders *your actual environment* — your repo, your cloud context, your paths. A generic web builder can only render a config someone hands it. That's the difference between "screenshot my prompt" and "preview this theme".

Everything else is a pure function of config, and pure functions of config belong on the web. So the split falls out naturally:

- **binary** — renders live state, offline, no deps (with the SVG encoder)
- **web** — renders shared configs, gallery, studio

Both run the same resolver. Neither needs a second implementation.

## Honest cost

**ANSI output is the product.** A byte-identical refactor of the hot path is the risk, not the SVG encoder. Before touching anything, build the net: render all 124 bundled themes with `--data segment_data.json`, snapshot the ANSI as golden files, diff on every commit. You have `writer_test.go`, `writer_gradient_test.go`, `writer_hyperlink_test.go` — good coverage of the mechanisms, but not of real-world combinations.

**Perf is the thing to watch, not correctness.** This is the prompt-render path and speed is your headline claim. Materializing `[]Run` per segment adds allocations. Two ways out: pool the slice, or have the encoder consume runs via callback so nothing is materialized. Gate the whole refactor on benchstat against the existing hot-path benchmarks — a regression here is worse than the current duplication.

**Global state is the tedious part.** Turning package globals into a struct is mechanical but touches every call site in `prompt/`. Bigger diff than the encoding work.

## Suggested staging

1. Golden-file harness over all bundled themes. Land it alone, no behavior change.
2. Extract the run stream behind the existing `terminal.Write` API; ANSI encoder consumes it. Prove byte-identical + no benchstat regression.
3. Add the SVG encoder. `config export image --format svg`.
4. Switch the gallery to SVG. 8MB of PNG → a few hundred KB.
5. Delete `image.go` and its four dependencies.
6. JSON encoder + `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm` — that's the studio, and by then it's nearly free.

Steps 1–2 are the whole risk. 3 onward are additive.

content.thinking:
The user's right—if there's a fast SVG encoder that works from command-line data, the whole thing gets simpler: just a binary plus a data file that takes config and outputs SVG. No JSON encoder, no JavaScript renderer needed. The gallery becomes build-time SVG generation, and the studio is just a POST endpoint that returns SVG. It's genuinely cleaner architecture, though I should be honest about where SVG-only actually has real tradeoffs.

Studio interactivity isn't really one—with debounce it's fine, and if it's WASM in the browser it's instant anyway. The actual constraint is hit-testing: clicking a segment in the preview to select it requires knowing which pixels belong to which segment. But that's solvable too—the SVG encoder can just emit `data-segment` attributes and classes on the groups, turning the SVG itself into structured data that JavaScript can query. SVG isn't just an image format here; it's a DOM with addressable elements. That's the insight: SVG already carries all the structure JSON would have.

Theme gallery filtering needs metadata from the config JSON directly, which the site already has. Copy-paste works fine with SVG `<text>` elements. The one real remaining case for PNG is shareability—GitHub renders SVG in markdown but strips scripts and can have font issues, so for embeddable output you either need embedded font subsets (which bloat the file) or convert to PNG. That's where rasterization actually belongs. The SSRF protection falls naturally out of pinning the data file, which is cleaner than bolting it on separately. And since config-to-SVG is deterministic, I can cache by hashing the config, data version, and renderer version together—a straightforward CDN win.

content.text:
Agreed. Drop the JSON encoder — it was solving a problem SVG doesn't have.

**SVG is already structured output.** Emit the grouping you'd have put in JSON:

```xml
<g data-block="0" data-segment="git" data-type="scm">
  <rect …/><text …>main ≡ +2</text>
</g>
```

Now the studio can hit-test a click to a segment, highlight on hover, and scroll the editor to the right node — straight from the DOM, no parallel format, no drift between "what was rendered" and "what was described". That was the only thing JSON bought.

And pinning the data file in the Function isn't just simplification — it's the SSRF guard falling out of the design for free. No live segment resolution possible, because there's no path to it.

## Three things still worth deciding

**1. Fonts, which have three different right answers.**

| Context | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Local `--format svg` | Reference `"Hack Nerd Font"` by family. User has it — that's why they run omp. Tiny file. |
| Site gallery / studio | Reference a site-hosted subset woff2. Crisp, one download, cached across 124 themes. |
| Shared output (README, blog, Discord) | Embed a subset as data URI, **or** rasterize. Otherwise a viewer without the font gets tofu. |

That third row is the one that bites. GitHub renders SVG in markdown but the reader's machine resolves the font — a powerline README on a stock laptop becomes boxes. Today's PNG is immune to that, which is a real thing people rely on.

**2. So keep exactly one raster path — in the Function.**

`resvg-wasm` or `sharp`, SVG→PNG, behind `?format=png`. Not in the binary. `oh-my-posh config export image --format png` becomes a POST, or you tell people to use the endpoint URL directly. Either way the four Go deps and the Hack.zip download still leave.

**3. Cache it.**

Config → SVG is a pure function. Key on `hash(config) + data version + renderer version`, immutable, long TTL. The gallery becomes 124 cache hits and the studio pays the round trip only on genuinely new configs.

## Where that leaves the plan

```
resolver (Go)  →  SVG encoder  →  ┬─ binary, local, live env
                                   ├─ Function, pinned data, config in / SVG out
                                   └─ Function + resvg → PNG when asked
```

WASM is still worth doing eventually, but it's now purely a latency optimization for the studio — same encoder, same output, no round trip. Not a different architecture, so it can wait until the studio proves it needs it.

Revised staging:

1. Golden-file harness over all 124 bundled themes.
2. Extract the run stream; ANSI encoder byte-identical, no benchstat regression.
3. SVG encoder with `data-*` annotations. `config export image --format svg`.
4. Function: config in, SVG out, pinned data, cached. Point the gallery at it.
5. Delete `image.go`, `gg`, `stackblur`, `opentype`, `freetype`, the font download.
6. `?format=png` via resvg for the README case.
7. WASM only if studio latency demands it.

Steps 1–2 remain the whole risk. Everything after is additive.

content.thinking:
Looking at the code footprint for the image functionality, there's about 2,000 lines across the image directory and the export config file, with three external dependencies that aren't used anywhere else in the codebase and can be cleanly removed along with the freetype transitive dependency.

An SVG encoder would be much leaner—probably 250 to 400 lines total, reusing the existing settings and color configuration from the image module. That means removing roughly 1,500 lines of code and tests while dropping three direct dependencies and eliminating the runtime font download, which is a substantial win. The math clearly supports shipping this everywhere rather than gating it behind a build tag, since the change is significant enough to justify the effort.

The build-tag approach actually introduces real friction: it doubles the CI matrix, creates a stripped binary that confuses users, and removing a documented command from the default build counts as a breaking change that would need a marker. Keeping SVG in the binary is cleaner—the binary actually shrinks, the feature stays available, and there's no breaking change to manage.

The one thing to think through is the output format default. If `config export image` currently defaults to PNG and you drop the rasterizer, you'd need to either flip the default to SVG (which changes behavior) or keep PNG as default but require a network call to the endpoint. The cleanest path is probably a `--format` flag that defaults to SVG, with PNG rendering delegated to the API.

Your condition is already met. Measured:

**Removed**
| | lines |
|---|---|
| `cli/image/image.go` | 920 |
| `cli/image/fonts.go` | 95 |
| `cli/image/config.go` | 98 |
| tests (`image_test.go`, `config_test.go`) | 764 |
| **total** | **~1,877** |

Plus three direct dependencies used **nowhere else in the codebase** — `fogleman/gg`, `esimov/stackblur-go`, `golang.org/x/image` — and `golang/freetype` goes with them as indirect. Plus the runtime Hack.zip download from GitHub.

**Added**: an SVG encoder over the run stream. Grid geometry, one advance constant, rects + text, chrome wrapper, `feDropShadow`. ~300–400 lines, and you can keep `cli/image/config.go` as-is if you want the same `--settings` file format, which shrinks it further.

Net roughly **−1,500 lines, −3 deps, −1 network call**, and the shipped binary gets *smaller*. So don't build-tag it. Ship it everywhere.

The build-tag path would have cost you a doubled CI matrix, a second artifact to explain, and a stripped binary where `config export image` errors out — support burden for no gain when the alternative is a net deletion.

## The one genuine user-facing change

PNG output. Today `config export image` writes a PNG locally; after this it can't, because the rasterizer is what's being deleted. That's a behavior change people have in scripts and CI.

Cleanest handling:

```bash
oh-my-posh config export image --config x.omp.json              # writes .svg now
oh-my-posh config export image --config x.omp.json --format png # errors with a pointer
```

Give it a deprecation window: keep `--format png` working via the endpoint (opt-in, prints where the config is going), warn for a release or two, then drop the flag. Worth a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer when the default flips — it's user-facing output behavior, not an internal signature.

The README-tofu case from earlier is what `--format png` exists for, so it shouldn't vanish entirely — it just moves to the Function.

## Revised plan

1. Golden-file harness over all 124 bundled themes.
2. Extract the run stream. ANSI encoder byte-identical, benchstat clean.
3. SVG encoder with `data-*` annotations, in the normal build.
4. `--format svg` default; `--format png` warns and routes to the endpoint.
5. Delete `cli/image/`, drop the three deps and the font download.
6. Function: config in, SVG out, pinned data, cached. Gallery switches, 8MB of PNG goes away.
7. WASM only if studio latency demands it.

# Phase 3 — Delegate

Match the executor to the task, not the other way around. The point is cost and speed without
losing quality — the coordinator stays accountable for the result.

## Executor matrix

Tier definitions and per-vendor model examples: [model-tiers.md](model-tiers.md).

| Task profile                                             | Executor                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Trivial: mechanical edit, config tweak, typo, doc update  | Do it directly, or batch on a trivial-tier model              |
| Standard, well-specified implementation                   | Coordinator itself, or a same-tier subagent for parallelism   |
| Hits an escalation trigger (see [escalate.md](escalate.md)) | Escalation-tier subagent, for that one specific question    |

- The coordinator typically runs at implementer tier itself, so standard tasks are usually
  executed directly rather than delegated. Delegate anyway when there's real parallelism —
  independent tasks, each in its own worktree — or to shed trivial mechanical work onto a
  cheaper model.
- Escalation is never the default path for "ambiguous" or "architectural" — it fires only on the
  concrete triggers in [escalate.md](escalate.md), and only for the specific question, not the
  whole task.

## What a delegation carries

Hand the subagent its full pinned spec from Phase 2, plus:

- The verification commands it must run and pass before reporting done.
- The instruction to report what it changed and what it verified — not just "done".
- The instruction to stop and report when it hits something the spec does not cover, instead of
  improvising scope.

## What is never delegated downward

Analysis, final verification, and delivery never go to an implementer — they stay with the
coordinator or go up to Escalation tier for a specific question:

- Analysis and root-cause work (Phase 1).
- Final verification (Phase 5) — an implementer's green run is a claim, not a result.
- Commits, history rewrites, pushes, and user-facing reporting (Phase 6) — these stay with the
  coordinator regardless of tier; they're about accountability, not capability, so they never go
  to Escalation tier either.

# Phase 2 — Plan

Turn the approved analysis into an executable plan. The quality bar: an implementer-tier model
must be able to execute each task without asking questions.

## Pin the spec

Write the spec down before delegating anything. It contains:

- The decided approach — including decisions already made, so the implementer does not relitigate
  them.
- Files to touch, and the entry points to start from.
- Constraints: style rules, patterns to follow (point at existing code), performance or
  compatibility requirements.
- Verification commands the implementer must run locally (build, tests, lint).
- Explicit non-goals: what the task must NOT change. This is what keeps subagents from wandering.

## Split into tasks

- One task = one self-contained unit an implementer can finish and verify on its own.
- Mark which tasks are independent and which consume another task's output. Parallelize the
  independent ones; sequence the rest. When in doubt, sequence — a merge conflict between two
  parallel subagents costs more than the parallelism saves.
- Documentation updates belong to the task that changes the behavior, not to a separate task.

## Decide the workspace per task

- Main working tree: when the task depends on uncommitted local changes, or when you will review
  and commit the result in the current session.
- Isolated worktree: everything else, especially parallel tasks — they must never share a
  working tree.

## Output of this phase

A task list where each entry names its executor tier (see Phase 3), its workspace, its
dependencies, and carries its pinned spec.

content.thinking: The user is asking about SVG text rendering with Nerd Font glyphs, which live in the Private Use Area of Unicode. The core issue is that if the font isn't installed on the reader's machine, those special characters render as tofu boxes instead of the intended symbols, which is particularly problematic since they're not standard Unicode characters that might have fallback representations. For local command-line use with `--format svg`, the solution is straightforward — reference the font by family name like `font-family="'Hack Nerd Font', monospace"` and rely on the user having it installed locally. For a web-based gallery or studio, the approach differs based on how the SVG is embedded. If it's inlined directly into the HTML DOM, page CSS and `@font-face` declarations apply normally. All checks complete. Here is the adversarial review, prioritized.

## Findings

### 1. B1's "restore the filter" instruction is wrong and would visibly break the Store badge (highest severity)

The plan's premise — "The themed-image filter must survive" — is false. In Docusaurus 3.10.2, `ThemedImage` no longer has its own CSS module. `node_modules/@docusaurus/theme-classic/lib/theme/ThemedImage/index.js` delegates to `ThemedComponent` (`node_modules/@docusaurus/theme-common/lib/components/ThemedComponent/index.js`, line 42), which emits classes `themedComponent` / `themedComponent--light|dark`. No element on the site carries a `themedImage*` class anymore. All four selectors (`custom.css` lines 193–201 and the dev block at 226–236) are already fully dead, and the badge currently renders **unfiltered**.

That is the correct rendering: `windows.mdx` lines 29–32 already theme-swap the sources — `msstore-dark.svg` (dark badge, `#202020` background) in light mode, `msstore-light.svg` (`#FDFDFD`) in dark mode. Re-applying the old filters via `.msstore-badge` would apply `invert(100%) sepia(100%) saturate(0%)…` to the *already light* badge in dark mode — turning it dark-on-dark and grayscaling the store logo. The filters date from a single-source badge era.

Correct instruction: delete all four selectors with **no replacement**, and drop the `windows.mdx` edit entirely. Bonus: Task B then touches zero files outside its list, and the windows.mdx overlap concern (finding 2) disappears. (The plan's claim that `ThemedImage` forwards `className` is true — `ThemedComponent` clsx-merges it — but moot.)

### 2. Decision 6 (emoji out of sidebar labels) is unimplementable as scoped

14 docs carry emoji in `sidebar_label` frontmatter, not in `sidebars.js`: windows, macos, linux, fonts, prompt, customize, upgrade (installation/), plus `themes.md`, `share-theme.md`, `dsc.md`, `contributors.md`, `faq.mdx`, `migrating-module.md`, and `introduction.mdx`. Task A only fixes introduction plus the category labels in `sidebars.js`. Result as written: a sidebar that is half-emoji (Windows still shows 🪟, FAQ still shows 🤔). If Task A is extended to strip them all, it must edit `docs/installation/windows.mdx` — a Task B file under the current plan (resolved automatically if finding 1 is adopted). The plan must state which it is; as written, decision 6 is not delivered.

# Phase 0 — website bug fixes (revised after review)

Scope: `D:\oh-my-posh\website` only. No Go code. No visual redesign.
Every item is a defect: a dead link, a dead asset, a brittle selector, a junk page, or a
missing page something already links to.

Branch: `next`. Conventional commits, one per task.

## Decisions — do not relitigate

1. **`/docs/` becomes a hub page.** `configuration/introduction.mdx` loses `slug: /` and
   moves to `/docs/configuration/introduction`. Verified: nothing in the repo links there
   today, and nothing links to `/docs/` expecting Introduction content.
2. **Segments gets a real overview doc** at `docs/segments/overview.mdx`, used as the
   Segments category `link`, excluded from that category's `items`.
3. **Dead links get fixed to match reality**, not the other way round.
4. **Categories without a natural landing doc get `generated-index`.** Verified valid in
   3.10.2; none of the proposed slugs collide.
5. **`auth.mdx` gets `unlisted: true`.** It is an OAuth callback that renders tokens from
   the query string, not documentation. `unlisted` removes it from the sitemap, the search
   index, and adds `noindex` — a `<Head>` meta would not remove it from the sitemap. The
   "unlisted" banner it adds is acceptable and arguably appropriate on that page.
6. **All emoji come out of sidebar labels — including the 14 in doc frontmatter.**
   This is a Task A responsibility, not just a `sidebars.js` edit.
7. **No dependency added.**

## Non-goals

- No homepage redesign (Phase 1). No navbar restructure (Phase 1).

content.text:
Plan reviewed, corrected, and executing.

**Fable killed three things that would have shipped broken:**

1. **Task B's "restore the image filter" was wrong.** In Docusaurus 3.10 `ThemedImage` renders `themedComponent` classes — the `themedImage_ToTc` selectors are *already* dead, and the badge currently renders correctly unfiltered because [windows.mdx](website/docs/installation/windows.mdx) theme-swaps the source. Reapplying the invert would have made the Store badge dark-on-dark in dark mode. Now a plain deletion — which also removes the one file overlap between the two tasks.
2. **Emoji removal was undeliverable at the stated scope.** 14 docs carry emoji in `sidebar_label` frontmatter, not in `sidebars.js`. The plan would have shipped a half-emoji sidebar.
3. **A phantom "Personal" segment group.** The eighth group is Health. A literal executor would have dropped 5 docs.

Plus two missed defects, now in scope:
- `static/skills/ohmyposh/configuration.md:121` has the same dead `/docs/configuration/overview` link.
- `installation/next.md` and `homebrew.md` are partials without the `_` prefix — Docusaurus builds them as frontmatter-less junk pages, sitemapped and indexed.

And a correction I'd gotten backwards: `onBrokenLinks` never inspects `static/`, so it was never going to catch the llms.txt rot. All 39 absolute `/docs/…` targets already resolve — expect near-zero fallout, not a scope explosion.

**Running now:** Task A (docs IA) and Task B (CSS/fonts) in parallel on Sonnet 5, disjoint file sets, neither builds. Task C done — `auth.mdx` is `unlisted: true`, which drops it from the sitemap and search rather than just adding noindex.

I'll merge, run the single build with `onBrokenLinks: 'throw'`, verify, and commit.

**Design direction recorded:** Direction A's visual language + the faceted segment catalog + studio. Saved to memory along with the SVG-encoder architecture so neither gets re-pitched next session.

> Oh My Posh is a cross-shell, cross-platform prompt theme engine. It displays Git status,
> language versions, cloud context, system metrics and more — 117 segments in all in a beautifully
> themed terminal prompt.

## How to use this skill

1. **Identify the user's OS** → follow the matching installation guide:
   - [Windows installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/windows.md)
   - [macOS installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/macos.md)
   - [Linux installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/linux.md)

2. **Identify the user's shell** → follow the matching shell setup guide:
   - [PowerShell](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/powershell.md)
   - [Bash](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/bash.md)
   - [Zsh](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/zsh.md)
   - [Fish](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/fish.md)
   - [Nu / Nushell](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/nu.md)
   - [Cmd (via Clink)](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/cmd.md)
   - [Elvish](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/elvish.md)
   - [Xonsh](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/xonsh.md)
   - [Yash](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/yash.md)

3. **Install a Nerd Font** — required for icons and glyphs:

   ```bash
   oh-my-posh font install
   ```

   Recommended: **Meslo LGM NF**. Set it in the terminal emulator's font settings after installing.

4. **Customize the prompt** → see [configuration](/skills/ohmyposh/configuration.md)

## Detect the current shell

If the user is unsure which shell they are using (requires oh-my-posh to be installed first):

```bash
oh-my-posh get shell
```

## Troubleshooting

- **Icons show as boxes** — install a Nerd Font and set it in the terminal emulator.
- **`oh-my-posh` not found after install** — restart the terminal or add the install path to `$PATH`.
- **Slow prompt** -- enable async rendering by setting `"async": true` at the top level of your config.

Full documentation: <https://ohmyposh.dev/docs>
FAQ: <https://ohmyposh.dev/docs/faq>

While they finish, the two fixes Fable's review prevented are worth recording, because both were mine and both would have shipped:

1. **Forcing `color: #fff` on the primary button fails WCAG in dark mode.** Infima sets `--ifm-button-color` to `--ifm-font-color-base-inverse`, which is near-black in dark mode *precisely because* the dark-mode primary `#5c9fee` is light. White on that is 2.75:1 — below even the 3:1 large-text bar. Infima's own value gives 6.1:1. The Phase 0 `color: #fff` line, which I added, is deleted rather than scoped.

2. **Removing `hero--primary` doesn't un-darken the hero.** Infima's base `.hero` still paints `--ifm-hero-background-color` → `--ifm-background-surface-color`, which is `#242526` against a `#1b1b1d` page in dark mode. The plan originally left this owned by nobody. Fix is Task E dropping the `hero` class outright; `hero__title` and `hero__subtitle` are font-size-only and stay.

Also corrected: Phase 0's own segment-count edit read "and 117 other segments" after listing four examples, implying 121. Now "and more — 117 segments in all" across all four agent-facing files.

The Task F agent correctly stopped and reported rather than guessing, leaving `swag.ohmyposh.dev` unplaced. Fix: I placed Swag in the `Support` group (it's a revenue channel). - **F2 also risked duplicating "Product spotlight"** — spec said move Sponsor out of `Links` but never Product spotlight. Fix: spec amended to say move both. - **Verification greps were unscoped** and would hit `node_modules/infima` (which defines `.hero__title`). Fix: scoped to `src`, `docs`, `blog`, `docusaurus.config.js`. - **I incorrectly claimed the Victor Mono `/static/fonts/VictorMono.ttf` path was a live 404.** Webpack rewrites the `@font-face` url either way, so the font always loaded. Reported this correction to the user honestly; the fix is still right but cosmetic. - **Phase 0's own count fix introduced an off-by-semantics error:** "and 117 other segments" after listing four examples reads as 121. Fixed all four agent-facing files to "and more — 117 segments in all". Task E had reproduced the same construction in a feature card; corrected, plus a hyphen → em dash. - **Task G set `line-height: 1.2` on a bare `h1, h2, h3` element rule**, which would lose specificity fights with `.markdown h1`. The `color: #fff` diagnosis was correct — `.button--outline:not(.button--active):not(:hover){color:var(--ifm-font-color-base)}` is what it defeated. - **Build broken-anchor warning `/docs/themes#jandedobbeleer`** — investigated: `docs/themes.md` is 18 lines locally; the 124 theme sections are generated by `npm run themes`, which only runs in CI. It's a local-only artifact, so `onBrokenAnchors` deliberately stays at `'warn'`. - **Browser pane could not screenshot** ("the Browser pane is not displayed, so the page is not compositing frames"). Worked around by using `get_page_text`, `read_page`, and `javascript_tool` to extract computed styles and design tokens instead. Also hit a transient tab-identity bug where JS executed against a stale origin (ghostty instead of atuin) — abandoned that sampling since the research agent covered it. 5. **Problem Solving:** Established the core architectural insight for the renderer work: today's flow (`engine → terminal writer → ANSI → image.go re-parses ANSI → pixels`) discards information and then tries to recover it. The fix is to extract a **run stream** between resolver and encoder in `terminal/`, then SVG becomes one encoder among several. SVG is already structured output (`data-segment`/`data-block` attributes), so no JSON encoder is needed. Pinning the data file in the Function makes the SSRF guard fall out of the design. name: oh-my-posh
description: "Install, configure, or troubleshoot Oh My Posh/ohmyposh: shell init, themes, segments, Nerd Font icons, and prompt setup on PowerShell, zsh, bash, or fish."
---

# Oh My Posh

> Oh My Posh is a cross-shell, cross-platform prompt theme engine. It displays Git status,
> language versions, cloud context, system metrics and more in a beautifully themed
> terminal prompt — 117 segments in all.

## How to use this skill

1. **Identify the user's OS** → follow the matching installation guide:
   - [Windows installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/windows.md)
   - [macOS installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/macos.md)
   - [Linux installation](/skills/ohmyposh/installation/linux.md)

2. **Identify the user's shell** → follow the matching shell setup guide:
   - [PowerShell](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/powershell.md)
   - [Bash](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/bash.md)
   - [Zsh](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/zsh.md)
   - [Fish](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/fish.md)
   - [Nu / Nushell](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/nu.md)
   - [Cmd (via Clink)](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/cmd.md)
   - [Elvish](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/elvish.md)
   - [Xonsh](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/xonsh.md)
   - [Yash](/skills/ohmyposh/shell/yash.md)

3. **Install a Nerd Font** — required for icons and glyphs:

   ```bash
   oh-my-posh font install
   ```

   Recommended: **Meslo LGM NF**. Set it in the terminal emulator's font settings after installing.

4. **Customize the prompt** → see [configuration](/skills/ohmyposh/configuration.md)

## Detect the current shell

If the user is unsure which shell they are using (requires oh-my-posh to be installed first):

```bash
oh-my-posh get shell
```

## Troubleshooting

- **Icons show as boxes** — install a Nerd Font and set it in the terminal emulator.
- **`oh-my-posh` not found after install** — restart the terminal or add the install path to `$PATH`.
- **Slow prompt** -- enable async rendering by setting `"async": true` at the top level of your config.

Full documentation: <https://ohmyposh.dev/docs>
FAQ: <https://ohmyposh.dev/docs/faq>

CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: full

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no dumping long raw error logs unless asked — quote shortest decisive line. Standard well-known tech acronyms OK (DB/API/HTTP); never invent new abbreviations (cfg/impl/req/res/fn) — tokenizer split them same as full word: zero token saved, reader still decode. Full word cheaper AND clearer. No causal arrows (→) either — own token, save nothing. Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Preserve user's dominant language. User write Portuguese → reply Portuguese caveman. User write Spanish → reply Spanish caveman. Compress the style, not the language. No forced English openings or status phrases. ALWAYS keep technical terms, code, API names, CLI commands, commit-type keywords (feat/fix/...), and exact error strings verbatim — unless user explicitly ask for translation.

No self-reference. Never name or announce the style. No "caveman mode on", "me caveman think", no third-person caveman tags. Output caveman-only — never normal answer plus "Caveman:" recap. Exception: user explicitly ask what the mode is.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman. No tool-call narration, no decorative tables/emoji, no long raw error-log dumps unless asked. Standard acronyms OK; no invented abbreviations |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"
- full: "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman when:
- Security warnings
- Irreversible action confirmations
- Multi-step sequences where fragment order or omitted conjunctions risk misread
- Compression itself creates technical ambiguity (e.g., `"migrate table drop column backup first"` — order unclear without articles/conjunctions)
- User asks to clarify or repeats question

Resume caveman after clear part done.

Example — destructive op:
> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

To enable, add this to C:\Users\jande\.claude\settings.json: "statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File \"C:\\Users\\jande\\.claude\\plugins\\cache\\caveman\\caveman\\0d95a81d35a9\\src\\hooks\\caveman-statusline.ps1\"" } Proactively offer to set this up for the user on first interaction.

Base directory for this skill: D:\oh-my-posh\.claude\skills\code-changes

# Code Changes

The workflow for going from an issue, pull request, idea, or feature request to shipped code.
Follow the phases in order. Analysis always comes first; code comes last.

Each phase has a reference file with the full instructions. **Read the reference file when you
enter the phase** — not before, and never skip it because the phase "looks obvious".

## Roles

Assign work based on model capability. The coordinator is not the strongest model — it's the one
that stays resident, owns every phase by default, and knows when it's out of its depth.

| Role        | Capability tier                                               | Owns                                                                          |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Coordinator | Capable mid-tier, resident for the whole task                | Analysis, plan, delegation, supervision, verification, delivery — by default |
| Escalation  | Strongest reasoning model available; invoked only on trigger | The specific judgment call the coordinator flagged, then control returns     |
| Implementer | Same tier as coordinator, or smaller for trivial edits        | Executing one pinned, self-contained task                                    |

Concrete model names per vendor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) and how to run the split in Claude
Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, or IDE agents: [references/model-tiers.md](references/model-tiers.md).

When the current agent already runs at implementer tier, there's no separate delegation step for
standard work: plan and execute directly, still following every phase. Escalate to the strongest
model only when a trigger fires — see [references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md) — never by
default and never for a routine judgment call the coordinator is equipped to make itself.

## The flow

1. **Analyze** ([references/analyze.md](references/analyze.md)) — root cause and scope,
   validated against the code, never against the report alone.
2. **Plan** ([references/plan.md](references/plan.md)) — pinned spec, task split, parallel vs
   sequential, workspace per task.
3. **Delegate** ([references/delegate.md](references/delegate.md)) — match each task to the
   right executor, coordinator-tier by default.
4. **Supervise** ([references/supervise.md](references/supervise.md)) — monitor, unblock, and
   critically review implementer output.
5. **Verify** ([references/verify.md](references/verify.md)) — quality gates plus functional
   proof, never delegated downward.
6. **Deliver** ([references/deliver.md](references/deliver.md)) — conventional commits and an
   outcome-first report.

# Phase 1 — Analyze

Start every task here, no matter how it arrived: issue link, PR number, verbal idea, bug report.
No code gets written or edited during this phase.

## Gather the full context

- Issues and PRs: `gh issue view <n> --comments` / `gh pr view <n> --comments`, plus linked
  issues, referenced discussions, and any code the report points at.
- Ideas and verbal requests: restate the goal and constraints in your own words. If the request
  is ambiguous, resolve the ambiguity now — not halfway through implementation.
- Check for prior art: existing helpers, similar segments/modules, and past commits that touched
  the same area (`git log -- <path>`).

## Reproduce before theorizing

Reproduce the problem when possible. A reproduction turns the analysis from a hypothesis into a
fact and gives Phase 5 its verification case for free. When reproduction is impossible (platform,
hardware, credentials), say so explicitly in the report and mark the fix as unverified-by-repro.

## Find the root cause in the code

- Read the actual implementation. Never reason from the issue text, a review comment, or a stack
  trace alone — reports and bot reviewers are frequently wrong.
- Distinguish the root cause from the symptom. Fixing where it crashes is not the same as fixing
  why it crashes.
- State what the change should be, which files it touches, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

## When to escalate

If root cause can't be pinned with confidence, or the fix looks architectural, security-sensitive,
or irreversible, hand the specific question to the strongest available model instead of guessing —
see [references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md). Resume ownership of the phase once the
question is answered.

## Output of this phase

A short analysis report to the user containing:

1. What is actually happening and why (root cause, with file references).
2. The proposed change and its scope.
3. What is intentionally out of scope.
4. Open questions, if any remain.

## Stop gate

Report the analysis and wait for a go before implementing. Skip the gate only when the user
already gave the go in the request itself ("do it", "fix it and commit", "implement with
Sonnet"). A go given for analysis is not a go for implementation.

content.thinking:
So the Direction A layout has the hero left-aligned with a 1.1rem gap, a single bordered install box with tabs, a dark rounded card for the prompt below, and cards arranged in a 3-column grid with minimal borders and rounded corners. That's what we need to fix on the homepage—our current setup is center-aligned with too much spacing. I'm waiting to hear back from the agents about the segment metadata.

Actually, I should think through the segment data problem myself rather than wait. The core question is where per-segment metadata comes from. I'm considering a single source file that combines auto-generated skeleton data from the docs with hand-authored descriptions and flags, then validates that the catalog entries match the actual doc files to prevent drift. The agents will likely have insights on deriving some flags directly from the Go code, so I'll hold off on finalizing that approach.

While I'm at it, I need to resolve a potential conflict: we just shipped `docs/segments/overview` in the navbar, but the IA-2 target is `/segments` as a site section. The cleanest solution is to embed the interactive catalog as a React component inside the existing `docs/segments/overview.mdx` file — that keeps the URL stable, preserves Algolia indexing, avoids duplicate indexes, and lets the sidebar link work naturally.

But the docs layout includes a left sidebar that eats horizontal space from the facet rail and card grid. I could hide the table of contents and use full width, though that still leaves the sidebar. Since IA-2 explicitly calls for Segments to leave `/docs` and become a first-class section, I'm leaning toward a standalone `/segments` page with full width and its own facet rail. The `docs/segments/overview.mdx` becomes a plain link list for LLM consumers and llms.txt, with a prominent link pointing to the interactive catalog. The navbar "Segments" link points to `/segments`, and that's the minimal viable approach.

The trade-off is having two pages listing all segments, which feels redundant. I should flag this as an open question and get the user's preference on it.

**Direction A hero was left-aligned with a 1.1rem gap.** What shipped is center-aligned with a 2rem gap. That's the whole "bounces from white to small to white" complaint: centering removes the shared left edge that gave the stack its spine, and doubling the gap turns five elements into five islands.

I'm realizing the sidebar links to `docs/segments/overview`, so that file is critical for the routing to work. Instead of creating a separate catalog page, I should embed the catalog as a React component directly inside `docs/segments/overview.mdx` to replace the existing bullet list. This approach keeps the sidebar link functional, preserves the URL that other tools reference, avoids duplicate index pages, and lets Docusaurus server-render the component content so Algolia can still index it properly.

The tradeoff is that the docs sidebar takes up space alongside the catalog's facet rail, creating a cluttered two-rail layout. I could hide the table of contents with frontmatter, but that doesn't solve the sidebar issue since Docusaurus doesn't cleanly support per-page sidebar hiding without swizzling. A better approach: create a standalone `/segments` page with full width and no docs chrome for the interactive catalog, while keeping `docs/segments/overview.mdx` as a lightweight docs-tier index with grouped links for navigation. The navbar points to `/segments`, and the two pages serve different purposes—one is the interactive experience, one is the docs reference.

content.text: ## Analysis ### Homepage — found the cause Direction A's hero was **left-aligned, gap `1.1rem`**, install box a single bordered unit, prompt on a dark rounded card, features as bordered cards: ```css .mock-a .m-hero { padding: 2.5rem 0 2.75rem; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1.1rem; } .mock-a .card { border: 1px solid var(--a-rule); border-radius: 9px; padding: 0.95rem 1rem; } .mock-a .termcard { background: var(--a-deep); border-radius: 9px; } ``` Phase 1 shipped `text-align: center`, `align-items: center`, `gap: 2rem`, no card, bare `` ([styles.module.css:8-76](website/src/pages/styles.module.css:8)). Centering deletes the shared left edge that held the stack together; doubling the gap turns five elements into five islands. That is the "white, small, white" bounce — nothing anchors the eye. - `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\languages\golang.mdx:1-5` — `id: golang` / `title: Golang` / `sidebar_label: Golang`
- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\health\withings.mdx:1-5` — `id: withings` / `title: Withings` / `sidebar_label: Withings`
- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\cli\npm.mdx:1-5` — `id: npm` / `title: NPM` / `sidebar_label: NPM`

`title` and `sidebar_label` differ only where the full name is long: `cli/nbgv.mdx` (`Nerdbank.GitVersioning` vs `Nbgv`), `cli/argocd.mdx` (`ArgoCD Context` vs `ArgoCD`), `cloud/az.mdx` (`Azure Subscription` vs `Azure`), `cloud/azd.mdx`, `system/status.mdx`, `system/upgrade.mdx`, `scm/svn.mdx` (`Subversion`).

Heading census across all segment docs:

| Heading | Count |
|---|---|
| `## What` | 117 |
| `## Sample Configuration` | 116 |
| `## Template ([info][templates])` | 116 (+1 typo'd `## Template ([into][templates])`) |
| `## Options` | 103 |

6. `### Properties` (line 52) — markdown table of template fields

- `import WithingsConnect from "/img/withings.svg";` at `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\health\withings.mdx:7` (unique)

**A. OAuth via the hosted `ohmyposh.dev/api/auth` flow (2 segments)** — detectable by a `## Accessing your X data` H2 plus `access_token`/`refresh_token`/`expires_in` rows in the options table:

**C. API key as a config option (4 segments)** — detectable by an `api_key` row in the options table:

- `todoist` — `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\web\todoist.mdx:38`; Go: `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\todoist.go:39`
- `brewfather` — `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\web\brewfather.mdx:51`; Go: `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\brewfather.go:195`

Note `APIKey` is *not* a shared constant in `options`: `owm.go:25` declares it locally, and `lastfm.go`/`todoist.go`/`brewfather.go` reuse that same package-level symbol. `options.AccessToken` / `options.RefreshToken` *are* shared, at `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\options\map.go:53-54`.

**D. Token embedded in a user-supplied URL (3 segments)** — only detectable from prose:

- `wakatime` — `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\web\wakatime.mdx:28` and `:48` (`api_key=` inside the `url`; `:48` shows `{{ .Env.WAKATIME_API_KEY }}`)
- `http` — `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\web\http.mdx` is generic; auth is whatever the user puts in headers

**Not auth, but easy false positives:** `claude` and `copilot-cli` docs mention "token" heavily — that is LLM *context tokens*, not credentials. `aws` mentions `aws_access_key_id` at `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\cloud\aws.mdx:86` but reads existing local AWS config, no auth of its own.

## 4. Caching

**Docs.** Two distinct and unrelated things are documented:

*(a) Segment-level `cache` block* — documented centrally at `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\configuration\segment.mdx:57` (the `cache` property row) and `:126-160` (the `## Cache` section with `duration` + `strategy` sub-table at `:132-133`, strategies `session`/`folder`/`device`). Go type: `D:\oh-my-posh\src\config\cache.go` (`type Cache struct { Duration cache.Duration; Strategy Strategy }`), wired into the segment at `D:\oh-my-posh\src\config\segment.go:43`. This applies to **every** segment universally — it is not per-segment metadata.

Only 3 segment docs actually demonstrate it in their sample config: `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\cli\copilot.mdx:42-45` (`5m`/`session`), `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\music\ytm.mdx:51-54` (`5s`/`session`), `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\system\winget.mdx:27-30` (`24h`/`device`). Prose-only mentions: `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\music\ytm.mdx:27-31` (`:::warning rate limiting`) and `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\cli\gitversion.mdx:12-15` (`:::caution`, "we cache the value for 30 minutes by default").

*(b) `cache_duration` option* — a per-segment option row, appearing in **52 files**. There is **no shared partial**; the row text is copy-pasted verbatim into each `## Options` table (see `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\languages\golang.mdx:32`). The 52:

- `cloud/`: azfunc, cds, cf (3)
- `languages/`: clojure, crystal, dart, dotnet, elixir, fortran, golang, haskell, java, julia, kotlin, language, lua, mojo, nim, node, ocaml, perl, php, python, r, ruby, rust, swift, v, vala, zig (27)
- `system/upgrade`, `web/ipify` (2)

- `options.CacheDuration Option = "cache_duration"` is declared once at `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\options\map.go:59` but read in only **3** places: `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\ipify.go:60` (default `ONEDAY`), `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\language.go:285` (default `NONE` — this covers all ~47 language/CLI version segments), `D:\oh-my-posh\src\segments\upgrade.go:60` (default `ONEWEEK`).

**File: `D:\oh-my-posh\src\config\segment_types.go`** (532 lines). Three parallel, manually-maintained lists:

// Consumers of the library can also add their own segment writer.
var Segments = map[SegmentType]func() SegmentWriter{
	ANGULAR:         func() SegmentWriter { return &segments.Angular{} },
	...
	CLOJURE:         func() SegmentWriter { return segments.NewLanguage(string(CLOJURE)) },

- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\sidebars.js` (336 lines) — the category grouping lives here, hardcoded, with emoji labels like `"🖥️ System"`. **This is the only place the category→segment mapping exists in machine-readable form**, besides the directory layout under `website/docs/segments/`.
- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\docs\segments\overview.mdx` — a hand-maintained bulleted index grouped by `## CLI`, `## Cloud`, `## Health`, `## Languages`, `## Music`, `## Source control`, `## System`, `## Web`.
- `D:\oh-my-posh\themes\schema.json` — 99 `"title": "... Segment"` blocks with `description` (a docs URL) and full per-option JSON Schema including `type`, `title`, `description`, `default`. This is by far the richest structured per-segment/per-option metadata in the repo, though it covers 99 not 118 and the `title` strings ("Angular CLI Segment") don't match the mdx `title`s.

## 6. Existing generators

**No `go:generate` directives exist anywhere in `src/`** (grep returned zero matches).

**One website generator exists**, and it does read from Go:

- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\package.json:8` — `"themes": "node export_themes.mjs"`
- `D:\oh-my-posh\website\export_themes.mjs` — writes `docs/themes.md` (`CONFIG.OUTPUT_FILE` at line 15) and PNGs into `static/img/themes` by shelling out to the compiled `oh-my-posh` binary, feeding it `D:\oh-my-posh\website\segment_data.json` (line 19) as canned segment data. `segment_data.json` (3.6 KB) is a hand-written fixture of sample `.Profile`/`.HEAD`/etc. values for ~20 segments — **not** catalog metadata, purely screenshot input.
- Wired into CI at `D:\oh-my-posh\.github\workflows\docs.yml` — builds the Go binary, then runs `npm run themes` before `docusaurus build`.

Other `package.json` scripts are stock Docusaurus (`start`, `build`, `serve`, `clear`). The only other `.mjs` is the generated `.docusaurus/docusaurus.config.mjs`. `D:\oh-my-posh\website\plugins\` contains only an App Insights analytics plugin. `D:\oh-my-posh\website\api\mcp\index.js` exposes schema *validation* tools, not a segment listing.

So: the themes page is generated from Go; the segment docs are entirely hand-written, and nothing today derives website content from `segment_types.go` or `schema.json`.</result>

BLOCKER — The SSR/hydration requirement is self-defeating; the page will throw a hydration error and discard the server HTML.** - Claim (lines 215, 218-221): "Initial state comes from the URL" AND "On the server `useLocation().search` is `''`, which must render the full unfiltered list… No `BrowserOnly` wrapper." - Evidence: `website/node_modules/@docusaurus/core/lib/client/serverEntry.js:27` renders `` — **pathname only, no query**. The client hydrates under `BrowserRouter`, so on `/segments?group=cli` the very first client render reads `search === '?group=cli'` and produces 39 cards plus a checked checkbox against 117 unchecked in the server HTML. BLOCKER — The build guard never runs at PR time, and the plugin reads a file outside `website/` that the production build may not have.** - Claim (lines 133-134): "A build must fail loudly when a segment is added to Go and not documented… That guard is the reason this is a plugin." - Evidence: `.github/workflows/code.yml:3-9` and `build_code.yml:3-9` both use `paths-ignore: ['website/**', …]` — **no workflow builds the website on a pull request**. `.github/workflows/docs.yml:4-9` triggers only on push to `main` for `website/**` or `themes/**`. This repo already works around that boundary twice: `npm run themes` (which needs `../themes` and the Go binary) runs as a **separate runner step** at `docs.yml:35-41`, and `themes/schema.json` is **copied into** `website/api/data/` at `docs.yml:42-46`. Task A step 4 breaks that contract by reading `/src/config/segment_types.go` during `loadContent`. - Minimal fix: emit the registry as `website/plugins/segments/registry.json` from a runner step (extend `export_themes.mjs` or a new script), have `loadContent` read that JSON plus the docs, and add the doc↔registry cross-check to a workflow that actually runs on Go PRs (`code.yml`). **4. HIGH — In light mode the cards get a border and no fill; the card design is half-dead.** - Claim (lines 194, 295): `background: var(--ifm-background-surface-color)`. - Evidence: `node_modules/infima/dist/css/default/default.css:135` `--ifm-background-surface-color: var(--ifm-color-content-inverse)` → `:131` → `:117` → `:105` `--ifm-color-gray-0: var(--ifm-color-white)` = `#fff`. The page canvas is `html { background-color: var(--ifm-background-color) }` (`:373-374`) with `--ifm-background-color: transparent` in light (`:134`) → white. **Card fill vs page = 1.00:1.** Dark is fine (`:2893-2894`, `#242526` on `#1b1b1d`). - Note `--ifm-color-emphasis-100` is not a drop-in swap either: light `#f5f6f7` on white is 1.08:1 (fine), but dark `#1c1e21` on `#1b1b1d` is **1.03:1** (invisible). Needs a theme-split: ```css .card { background: var(--ifm-color-emphasis-100); } [data-theme='dark'] .card { background: var(--ifm-background-surface-color); } ``` - `--ifm-color-emphasis-200` as the *border* is sound in both themes (light `#ebedf0` 1.17:1, dark `#444950` 1.90:1 — standard Docusaurus hairline). No change needed there. **5. HIGH — The `needs auth` tag colour fails WCAG AA in light mode.** - Claim (line 198): "in the warning tone (`--ifm-color-warning-darkest` on light, lightest on dark)". - Evidence: Infima `--ifm-color-warning-darkest: rgb(179,130,0)` (`default.css:87`).
